# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

1	# Design brief
2	
3	The source of taste for the design system. Every token, component and generated screen is built against this page. Where it speaks, it overrides `frontend-design` and any other default.
4	
5	## Personality: warm, assured, plain-spoken
6	
7	The product moves other people's money, so it has to feel trustworthy without feeling cold. Warmth lives in colour, copy and softened corners; assurance lives in precise, quiet type; motion is the one loud thing. When a case isn't covered here, pick whatever is most warm, assured and plain-spoken.
8	
9	## Who it's for
10	
11	Two people use the screens, and density follows who's looking.
12	
13	| | Admin: working density | Contractor: full room |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| Row height | 46px | 60px |
16	| Body text | 14px | 16px |
17	| Label text | 14px | 16px |
18	| Page padding | 28px | 36px |
19	| Minimum target | 24px | 44px |
20	
21	- **Admin screens are dense.** _Why: the admin is the primary user and clears dozens of invoices a day on a desktop._
22	- **Contractor screens have room.** _Why: the contractor visits a few times a month, often on a phone, and wants reassurance more than throughput._
23	- 24px is a floor, not an exemption: targets still meet WCAG 2.2 target size, spacing rule included.
24	- Warmth is the same at both densities; only size and spacing change. See [ADR 0001](adr/0001-density-by-audience.md).
25	
26	## References (principles, never pixels)
27	
28	- **Stripe Dashboard**: how money and status read in dense tables.
29	- **Gusto**: warmth that still works for a payroll admin.
30	- **Linear**: motion only when the user acts, never as decoration.
31	
32	## Type
33	
34	One quiet family; hierarchy comes from size and weight, not from a second face.
35	
36	- **Instrument Sans** for everything, titles and amounts included, weights 400 and 600 only. _Why: neutral and precise, so colour, copy and motion carry the warmth; two weights keep hierarchy honest._
37	- Titles (24px and up) and a single large figure use 600 with slightly tightened tracking (about −0.015em, −0.02em for the figure). There is no display face.
38	- Scale on a 14px base, ratio about 1.2: 12, 14, 16, 20, 24, 32. Nothing off the scale.
39	- Sentence case everywhere. No ALL-CAPS labels or table headers; headers are 12px, 600, `ink-muted`.
40	- **Amounts** always use tabular figures, show cents, and right-align in tables. In tables: `4,800.00 USD`. On a single-currency card: `$4,800.00`. _Why: multi-currency lists must be impossible to misread, and digits must line up._
41	
42	## Colour
43	
44	Colour is assigned by role; components never name a hue.
45	
46	- **Roles**: `page`, `surface`, `surface-raised`, `ink`, `ink-muted`, `line`, `accent`, `on-accent`, `selected`, and status pairs for `awaiting`, `overdue`, `paid`, `scheduled`, `failed`.
47	- **State roles**: `accent-hover` and `accent-pressed` deepen the accent; `surface-hover` and `surface-pressed` deepen a neutral control; `control` is the 3:1 edge of an input or secondary button (`line` stays a hairline between surfaces); `disabled` and its text are a flat, quiet neutral; `scrim` sits behind overlays. Each has its own value in dark mode.
48	- **One accent, heather** (about `#80527A` light, `#D8B4D2` dark): a dusty berry for primary actions, selection and focus only. _Why: one accent keeps "what can I do here" obvious._
49	- **The focus ring shows on keyboard focus only** (`:focus-visible`), never on click. _Why: a ring on a clicked button reads as "selected"._
50	- **Status colours are their own set** and never borrow the accent:
51	
52	  | Awaiting | Overdue | Paid | Scheduled | Failed |
53	  |---|---|---|---|---|
54	  | Amber | Red | Green | Blue | Solid red |
55	
56	- **Colour alone never communicates state.** Every status tag carries its word. _Why: a colour-blind admin must still tell overdue from paid._
57	- **Every neutral is tinted toward plum.** No pure grey. Text is a plum-tinted ink (about `#2C2430`), never `#000`. _This deliberately opts into tinted ink for text, which `frontend-design` lists as a default._
58	- **Light is primary.** Dark gives every role its own value; it is not an inversion. Dark `page` is a deep plum-tinted dark, not black; surfaces get lighter as they rise; the accent lightens until it passes AA.
59	- WCAG AA in both themes: body text 4.5:1, large text 3:1, focus rings and the edges that identify a control 3:1.
60	
61	## Space, radius, elevation
62	
63	- **Spacing** on a 4px base, named steps only: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64. Off-scale values fail lint.
64	- **Radius by role, subtle, never a pill**:
65	
66	  | Buttons, segmented filters | Inputs, selects | Status tags, checkboxes | Surfaces, admin | Surfaces, contractor | Avatars |
67	  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
68	  | 6px | 6px | 4px | 8px | 12px | Round |
69	
70	  Nothing is fully rounded except avatars. Nested corners stay concentric (inner = outer − padding). _Why: softened corners keep some warmth without the friendly-app look; one radius everywhere is a default, not a choice._
71	- **Elevation, three levels**: flat (page and cards, separated by a `line` hairline), raised (sticky and floating bars, toasts: one soft plum-tinted shadow), overlay (modal, sheet, menu: a deeper shadow and a scrim). A shadow means "this floats", never "this is a box". In dark mode, levels are lighter surfaces.
72	
73	## Motion
74	
75	Motion confirms what the user just did. It is the system's signature, so it is precise rather than plentiful.
76	
77	- **Durations**: `fast` 120ms (press, hover colour), `base` 240ms (state change, selection), `slow` 320ms (sheet, modal, toast entering). Exits run at about 70% of the enter duration.
78	- **Easings**: `standard` (ease-out) by default; `exit` (ease-in) for leaving; `settle`, a single overshoot of about 4% with no second swing, only for confirming something the user did (a status flipping after pay, a toast arriving). Never on exits, never on anything the system starts.
79	- **Expected**: selection, the bulk-action bar entering and handing off to its toast, status changes staggered across rows, sheets opening from their trigger, a pending action's progress edge.
80	- **Banned**: bounce or elastic easing (more than one swing), entrance animations on page load, hover lift on cards or rows, anything that loops.
81	- **The one loop**: a pending action shows a progress edge along its button's bottom that fills once over `slow`. If the operation is still running, the edge sweeps until the result arrives, then stops. _Why: the wait has no known length, and a still button reads as frozen._ Reduced motion: a static edge.
82	- **Signature transitions**: (1) pay → the bar shows pending → once the payment is confirmed, statuses flip in a stagger and the bar becomes the toast; (2) a row expands into the invoice-detail sheet.
83	- **Never show success before it's confirmed.** The stagger is the confirmation, not a guess. _Why: assured means the screen never claims money moved when it hasn't._
84	- **Reduced motion**: no movement, overshoot or stagger; changes become a `fast` crossfade. Everything works without animation.
85	
86	## Icons and copy
87	
88	- **Phosphor**, regular weight: 16px on admin screens, 20px on contractor screens.
89	- **Copy** is second person, active and specific: "Your money is on its way", "Approve and pay", "Arrives Oct 20", never "soon". No exclamation marks, no emoji, no jokes in errors. Errors say what happened and what to do next. Admin copy is terser; the warmth stays.
90	
91	## Banned
92	
93	Named here so the brief stands on its own.
94

# Design brief

The source of taste for the design system. Every token, component and generated screen is built against this page. Where it speaks, it overrides `frontend-design` and any other default.

## Personality: warm, assured, plain-spoken

The product moves other people's money, so it has to feel trustworthy without feeling cold. Warmth lives in colour, copy and softened corners; assurance lives in precise, quiet type; motion is the one loud thing. When a case isn't covered here, pick whatever is most warm, assured and plain-spoken.

## Who it's for

Two people use the screens, and density follows who's looking.

| | Admin: working density | Contractor: full room |
|---|---|---|
| Row height | 46px | 60px |
| Body text | 14px | 16px |
| Label text | 14px | 16px |
| Page padding | 28px | 36px |
| Minimum target | 24px | 44px |

- **Admin screens are dense.** _Why: the admin is the primary user and clears dozens of invoices a day on a desktop._
- **Contractor screens have room.** _Why: the contractor visits a few times a month, often on a phone, and wants reassurance more than throughput._
- 24px is a floor, not an exemption: targets still meet WCAG 2.2 target size, spacing rule included.
- Warmth is the same at both densities; only size and spacing change. See [ADR 0001](adr/0001-density-by-audience.md).

## References (principles, never pixels)

- **Stripe Dashboard**: how money and status read in dense tables.
- **Gusto**: warmth that still works for a payroll admin.
- **Linear**: motion only when the user acts, never as decoration.

## Type

One quiet family; hierarchy comes from size and weight, not from a second face.

- **Instrument Sans** for everything, titles and amounts included, weights 400 and 600 only. _Why: neutral and precise, so colour, copy and motion carry the warmth; two weights keep hierarchy honest._
- Titles (24px and up) and a single large figure use 600 with slightly tightened tracking (about −0.015em, −0.02em for the figure). There is no display face.
- Scale on a 14px base, ratio about 1.2: 12, 14, 16, 20, 24, 32. Nothing off the scale.
- Sentence case everywhere. No ALL-CAPS labels or table headers; headers are 12px, 600, `ink-muted`.
- **Amounts** always use tabular figures, show cents, and right-align in tables. In tables: `4,800.00 USD`. On a single-currency card: `$4,800.00`. _Why: multi-currency lists must be impossible to misread, and digits must line up._

## Colour

Colour is assigned by role; components never name a hue.

- **Roles**: `page`, `surface`, `surface-raised`, `ink`, `ink-muted`, `line`, `accent`, `on-accent`, `selected`, and status pairs for `awaiting`, `overdue`, `paid`, `scheduled`, `failed`.
- **State roles**: `accent-hover` and `accent-pressed` deepen the accent; `surface-hover` and `surface-pressed` deepen a neutral control; `control` is the 3:1 edge of an input or secondary button (`line` stays a hairline between surfaces); `disabled` and its text are a flat, quiet neutral; `scrim` sits behind overlays. Each has its own value in dark mode.
- **One accent, heather** (about `#80527A` light, `#D8B4D2` dark): a dusty berry for primary actions, selection and focus only. _Why: one accent keeps "what can I do here" obvious._
- **The focus ring shows on keyboard focus only** (`:focus-visible`), never on click. _Why: a ring on a clicked button reads as "selected"._
- **Status colours are their own set** and never borrow the accent:

  | Awaiting | Overdue | Paid | Scheduled | Failed |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Amber | Red | Green | Blue | Solid red |

- **Colour alone never communicates state.** Every status tag carries its word. _Why: a colour-blind admin must still tell overdue from paid._
- **Every neutral is tinted toward plum.** No pure grey. Text is a plum-tinted ink (about `#2C2430`), never `#000`. _This deliberately opts into tinted ink for text, which `frontend-design` lists as a default._
- **Light is primary.** Dark gives every role its own value; it is not an inversion. Dark `page` is a deep plum-tinted dark, not black; surfaces get lighter as they rise; the accent lightens until it passes AA.
- WCAG AA in both themes: body text 4.5:1, large text 3:1, focus rings and the edges that identify a control 3:1.

## Space, radius, elevation

- **Spacing** on a 4px base, named steps only: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64. Off-scale values fail lint.
- **Radius by role, subtle, never a pill**:

  | Buttons, segmented filters | Inputs, selects | Status tags, checkboxes | Surfaces, admin | Surfaces, contractor | Avatars |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | 6px | 6px | 4px | 8px | 12px | Round |

  Nothing is fully rounded except avatars. Nested corners stay concentric (inner = outer − padding). _Why: softened corners keep some warmth without the friendly-app look; one radius everywhere is a default, not a choice._
- **Elevation, three levels**: flat (page and cards, separated by a `line` hairline), raised (sticky and floating bars, toasts: one soft plum-tinted shadow), overlay (modal, sheet, menu: a deeper shadow and a scrim). A shadow means "this floats", never "this is a box". In dark mode, levels are lighter surfaces.

## Motion

Motion confirms what the user just did. It is the system's signature, so it is precise rather than plentiful.

- **Durations**: `fast` 120ms (press, hover colour), `base` 240ms (state change, selection), `slow` 320ms (sheet, modal, toast entering). Exits run at about 70% of the enter duration.
- **Easings**: `standard` (ease-out) by default; `exit` (ease-in) for leaving; `settle`, a single overshoot of about 4% with no second swing, only for confirming something the user did (a status flipping after pay, a toast arriving). Never on exits, never on anything the system starts.
- **Expected**: selection, the bulk-action bar entering and handing off to its toast, status changes staggered across rows, sheets opening from their trigger, a pending action's progress edge.
- **Banned**: bounce or elastic easing (more than one swing), entrance animations on page load, hover lift on cards or rows, anything that loops.
- **The one loop**: a pending action shows a progress edge along its button's bottom that fills once over `slow`. If the operation is still running, the edge sweeps until the result arrives, then stops. _Why: the wait has no known length, and a still button reads as frozen._ Reduced motion: a static edge.
- **Signature transitions**: (1) pay → the bar shows pending → once the payment is confirmed, statuses flip in a stagger and the bar becomes the toast; (2) a row expands into the invoice-detail sheet.
- **Never show success before it's confirmed.** The stagger is the confirmation, not a guess. _Why: assured means the screen never claims money moved when it hasn't._
- **Reduced motion**: no movement, overshoot or stagger; changes become a `fast` crossfade. Everything works without animation.

## Icons and copy

- **Phosphor**, regular weight: 16px on admin screens, 20px on contractor screens.
- **Copy** is second person, active and specific: "Your money is on its way", "Approve and pay", "Arrives Oct 20", never "soon". No exclamation marks, no emoji, no jokes in errors. Errors say what happened and what to do next. Admin copy is terser; the warmth stays.

## Banned

Named here so the brief stands on its own.

- **Fonts**: Inter, Geist, Roboto, Arial, Space Grotesk.
- **Palette**: Tailwind palette names or values as the palette; purple or indigo gradients; terracotta or clay; cream backgrounds (~`#F4F1EA`); high-contrast display serifs.
- **Silhouettes**: shadcn defaults; one radius everywhere; pill-shaped buttons, tags or chips; the 8px-grid indigo button.
- **From `frontend-design`**, restated:
  1. Accenting one word in a headline with italic, bold or colour.
  2. All caps for labels.
  3. Unnecessary typographic labels above content.
  4. Numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the content is a real sequence.
  5. Big number + small label + supporting stats + gradient as the default hero.
  6. Fade-and-slide-up entrances on sections; hover transitions on every card.
  7. The font families you'd reach for on any other project.
  8. Warm cream background + high-contrast serif display + terracotta accent.
  9. Near-black background + a single acid-green or vermilion accent.
  10. Broadsheet: hairline rules, zero radius, dense newspaper columns.
  11. The SaaS-card kit: identical rounded cards, one radius, one `rgba(0,0,0,.1)` shadow, gradient washes.
  12. Template chrome: tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrows, `A · B · C` meta strings, `WORD — fragment` labels, monospace for small data labels, `→` appended to links and buttons. (Tinted ink for text is the one item opted into, above.)

## Calls I'd hand to a designer

I made these and would want a designer's eye on them first:

- The heather accent: does it carry primary actions on a busy screen?
- Instrument Sans alone, with no display face: is there enough hierarchy and warmth?
- Two densities instead of one.
- The plum tint on every neutral.

# Density follows the audience, not the component

Generated screens serve two people: the admin, who processes many contractor invoices a day, and the contractor, who visits a few times a month. The design brief picks a warm tone, which at full size slows down a dense invoice list. Rather than give up the warmth or the admin's throughput, the design system has two **density sets** (working density for admin screens, full room for contractor screens). They change only row heights, container padding, body size, icon size, surface radius and minimum target size. Colour, type families, radius roles, elevation and motion are shared.

## Considered options

- **One warm, roomy density everywhere**: rejected because it slows down the primary user.
- **Make the contractor the primary user**: rejected because the invoice list and bulk pay, the screens a design-systems evaluator scrutinises most, are admin screens.
- **One dense density everywhere**: rejected because contractor screens lose the reassurance the tone is meant to give, and 24px targets are too small on a phone.

## Consequences

Each screen brief has to say which audience it serves, so the right density set applies and gates can check against it. How components receive their density set is left to the component-build decisions.
# Tokens are the only styling vocabulary, and ESLint alone enforces it

The component library is built on Radix Primitives and Tailwind v4. The token build emits `@theme inline { --*: initial; … }`, so Tailwind's default palette and scale don't exist: the only classes that compile are the ones our tokens define, mapped to mode-aware `--ds-*` variables. That gives the agent a closed vocabulary, so generating `bg-gray-100 p-6 rounded-lg` becomes an immediate, specific failure the repair loop can act on. Token lint (gate 2) is ESLint only, in three layers: core rules (no `style`, no raw SVG colours, imports only through the library barrel, no Radix outside the library); `eslint-plugin-better-tailwindcss` (`no-unknown-classes` against our own theme file, `no-restricted-classes` for arbitrary values, `-(--x)` and bare numbers, `no-concatenated-classes`); and `@eslint/css` + `tailwind-csstree` with our own `no-raw-css-values` rule for `.css` files and `@apply`. A fixture of planted violations is kept as a test of the lint config, so a plugin upgrade can't quietly open a hole. Findings are in [Research styling approach and token lint options](https://github.com/gianko/design-demo/issues/4).

## Decisions that come with it

- **Library components take no `className`.** They change appearance only through typed variant props, so the registry describes everything a screen can change. Stack and Grid take token-union props for layout spacing.
- **Variants are written with `tailwind-variants/lite`**, one `tv()` per component with a slot for each Radix part. Nothing merges classes and `tailwind-merge` is never installed: it silently drops custom size tokens (`twMerge("text-caption text-fg")` → `"text-fg"`).
- **Density is a CSS scope.** `data-density="admin|contractor"` on a screen root flips the density variables; components use density-role tokens and never know which density they're in. This answers the open consequence of [ADR 0001](0001-density-by-audience.md).
- **Theme is an explicit `data-theme="light|dark"` attribute**, light by default, so Storybook, visual baselines and Figma captures can pin a mode. No automatic OS following in P0.
- **Bare-value families get named utilities**: `duration-{fast,base,slow}` plus exit variants, `ease-{standard,exit,settle}`, `z-{raised,overlay,toast}`, and one `delay-stagger` step. `opacity-*` is banned; disabled states use colour roles.
- **Motion is CSS only**: token utilities and keyframes, the View Transitions API for the two signature transitions, and stagger owned by the library (`:nth-child` × `delay-stagger`), so the `style` ban has no exceptions. Motion (the library) is the fallback if View Transitions can't carry the row → sheet transition with a Radix Dialog.

## Considered options

- **CSS modules**: smaller lint surface and no dependencies, but each generated screen becomes two files, class names are agent-invented with typos that still type-check, and there's no closed vocabulary for the repair loop.
- **Stylelint**: caught raw CSS values with no custom code, but can't see TSX classes or `@apply`, and would add a second tool to the repair loop.
- **`eslint-plugin-tailwindcss`**: missed arbitrary properties (`[color:#f00]`), the `p-(--x)` shorthand and template-literal classes.
- **`cva`**: what models write by default, but it has no slots, so every Radix part needs its own `cva()` kept in step by hand, and 1.0 is still in beta.
- **A `density` prop or Tailwind density variants**: every component would carry density logic, and class strings would double.
- **Motion (the library) by default**: built for shared-element transitions, but its JS-number props open a second raw-value surface for token lint.

## Consequences

Radix + Tailwind + variants is the shadcn stack, so the stack itself does nothing to prevent shadcn silhouettes. The design brief's ban on them is enforced by the brief and by taste lint.
# The generator is two Messages API calls, not an agent loop

Screens are generated by a fixed two-step workflow on the Messages API: `messages.parse()` with a Zod schema turns a screen brief into a UI spec, and a second call turns that UI spec into TSX, with gates run locally between and after them. The model never chooses a tool or explores files, so an agent harness gives it nothing to use. The gates, repair policy and eval accounting are ours whichever runtime runs them, so the direct API is the least code (~100–150 lines, `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `zod` only) and the most repeatable: we own the exact system prompt, parameters and transcript. This narrows demo brief §3's "reuse the agent-quiz-app pattern": the design system is still built by the unattended, issue-tracked Claude Code build loop, but one rep of a screen brief in an eval run isn't an issue, so the generator keeps "unattended" and "spec-first" and drops "issue-tracked". Findings are in [Research agent runtime options](https://github.com/gianko/design-demo/issues/5).

## Decisions that come with it

- **API key, not the subscription.** The Messages API can't authenticate with a claude.ai subscription. The key lives in a gitignored `.env`, with a Console spend limit (~$50/month) as the hard backstop. Eval runs don't draw on the subscription the build loop needs.
- **`claude-opus-5-5` for both steps**, effort `medium` for the spec step and `high` for the code step, set explicitly (Opus 5.5 can't disable thinking). Model and effort sit in one per-step config so an eval comparison can vary them like prompt and registry versions.
- **Zod**, through `zodOutputFormat()`, which converts the schema for the request and validates and parses the response. ArkType has no helper, and its responses would go unvalidated.
- **The wire schema is flat.** Structured outputs reject recursive schemas and cap a request at 24 optional and 16 union-typed parameters, so the UI spec sent to the API is a flat node list. The exact per-component prop check lives in the registry gate (gate 1), run locally. Both schemas are shaped in [Decide UI spec schema and registry generation](https://github.com/gianko/design-demo/issues/11).
- **Repair turns are append-only.** A failing step's response goes back onto its own `messages` array unchanged, followed by a user turn listing the gate failures. Earlier turns are never edited, as preserved thinking requires.
- **The code step sees the UI spec and the screen brief.** The UI spec is what the code must follow; the screen brief rides along as context for intent, copy and motion, so a code-step repair still has the original screen brief.
- **Cost is computed, not estimated.** Each attempt logs its `usage`, priced from a table checked into the repo. The design brief and registry form a cached `system` prefix shared across reps.
- **A `tsx` CLI** that the eval runner calls directly.

## Considered options

- **Claude Agent SDK**: has structured output, follow-up turns, cost fields and unattended mode, but saves no code, adds a bundled Claude Code binary and settings it loads from disk that must be switched off, and reports costs the docs call "client-side estimates".
- **The agent-quiz-app Ralph loop as-is**: picks one GitHub issue, implements it and closes it. It has no schema-constrained output, gate failures reach it only through git log and issue text, and it discards cost data. Right for the build loop, wrong for the generator.
- **Headless Claude Code (`claude -p`) on the subscription**: no per-token bill, but `--bare` turns off subscription login, so isolating runs from the repo's settings rests on untested flags. Schema output is validate-and-re-prompt, not constrained. It's undocumented whether `--resume` combines with `--json-schema`. Costs are estimates. Eval runs would share 5-hour and weekly limits with the build loop and could stop partway.
- **Both, behind one model-client interface**: about 50 more lines and two behaviours to keep matched, for a saving P0 doesn't need. Cheap to add later if spend becomes a problem.
- **Adding tools to the code step**: deferred. If it later needs them (e.g. looking up component docs), the SDK tool runner fits in without changing the shape.
# The UI spec is a flat, library-only node list, checked against a Zod-first registry

# Density follows the audience, not the component

Generated screens serve two people: the admin, who processes many contractor invoices a day, and the contractor, who visits a few times a month. The design brief picks a warm tone, which at full size slows down a dense invoice list. Rather than give up the warmth or the admin's throughput, the design system has two **density sets** (working density for admin screens, full room for contractor screens). They change only row heights, container padding, body size, icon size, surface radius and minimum target size. Colour, type families, radius roles, elevation and motion are shared.

## Considered options

- **One warm, roomy density everywhere**: rejected because it slows down the primary user.
- **Make the contractor the primary user**: rejected because the invoice list and bulk pay, the screens a design-systems evaluator scrutinises most, are admin screens.
- **One dense density everywhere**: rejected because contractor screens lose the reassurance the tone is meant to give, and 24px targets are too small on a phone.

## Consequences

Each screen brief has to say which audience it serves, so the right density set applies and gates can check against it. How components receive their density set is left to the component-build decisions.

The component library is built on Radix Primitives and Tailwind v4. The token build emits `@theme inline { --*: initial; … }`, so Tailwind's default palette and scale don't exist: the only classes that compile are the ones our tokens define, mapped to mode-aware `--ds-*` variables. That gives the agent a closed vocabulary, so generating `bg-gray-100 p-6 rounded-lg` becomes an immediate, specific failure the repair loop can act on. Token lint (gate 2) is ESLint only, in three layers: core rules (no `style`, no raw SVG colours, imports only through the library barrel, no Radix outside the library); `eslint-plugin-better-tailwindcss` (`no-unknown-classes` against our own theme file, `no-restricted-classes` for arbitrary values, `-(--x)` and bare numbers, `no-concatenated-classes`); and `@eslint/css` + `tailwind-csstree` with our own `no-raw-css-values` rule for `.css` files and `@apply`. # Button: component plan

**Use**: the one action a person takes from here: approve, pay, save, send. Reach for `primary` for the single main action on a screen or bar, `secondary` for the rest. Not for navigation (a link) or for filters (segmented filter).

## Anatomy

A native `<button>`, no Radix primitive: a button has no behaviour Radix adds. `tv()` slots:

- `root`: the button.
- `icon`: optional leading Phosphor icon (regular weight), `aria-hidden`.
- `label`: the visible text; it is the accessible name.
- `edge` and `sweep`: the pending progress edge along the bottom (only while pending).

## Variants, sizes, states

- **`intent`: `primary` | `secondary`.** Brief: "one accent, heather … for primary actions"; `control` is "the 3:1 edge of an input or secondary button". No ghost, no destructive: the brief names neither (see GAPS).
- **No size prop.** Size follows the density set ([ADR 0001](../../../../docs/adr/0001-density-by-audience.md)): `text-label` 14/16px, `min-h-target` 24/44px, `size-icon` 16/20px.
- **States**, each visibly distinct from rest:
  - rest; hover (deeper fill); pressed (deeper still); focus-visible (2px heather outline, offset 2px);
  - disabled: flat quiet neutral fill and text, edge dropped ("`disabled` and its text are a flat, quiet neutral");
  - pending: keeps its intent colours, ignores hover/press, shows the progress edge ("a pending action shows a progress edge along its button's bottom").

## Token map

| Slot · state | primary | secondary |
|---|---|---|
| root, base | `relative inline-flex min-h-target min-w-target items-center justify-center gap-2xs overflow-hidden rounded-control border px-sm py-3xs text-label transition-colors duration-fast ease-standard focus-visible:focus-ring` | same |
| root, rest | `border-transparent bg-accent text-on-accent` | `border-control bg-surface text-ink` |
| root, hover | `hover:bg-accent-hover` | `hover:bg-surface-hover` |
| root, pressed | `active:bg-accent-pressed` | `active:bg-surface-pressed` |
| root, disabled | `border-transparent bg-disabled text-disabled cursor-not-allowed` | same |
| root, pending | `cursor-progress`, no hover/pressed classes | same |
| icon | `size-icon shrink-0` | same |
| edge | `absolute inset-x-0 bottom-0 h-edge origin-left animate-progress-fill overflow-hidden` | same |
| sweep | `block size-full bg-on-accent animate-progress-sweep` | `… bg-accent …` |

## A11y contract

- Role `button` (native); accessible name is the label text; the icon is `aria-hidden`.
- Enter and Space activate (native). Focus ring on `:focus-visible` only, never on click.
- Disabled: native `disabled`, out of the tab order; nothing to announce.
- Pending: `aria-busy="true"` and `aria-disabled="true"`, stays focusable so keyboard focus doesn't drop to the page mid-operation; clicks are swallowed.
- Target: `min-h-target min-w-target`, 24px admin (rendered 30px tall), 44px contractor.

## Motion

- Hover and press: background colour over `duration-fast` + `ease-standard` ("fast 120ms: press, hover colour").
- Pending: `edge` fills once over `slow` (`animate-progress-fill`), then `sweep` slides along it until `pending` turns false (`animate-progress-sweep`). The brief's one loop.
- Reduced motion: tokens.css strips animations, so the edge renders full and still ("a static edge"); colour changes stay a `fast` crossfade.

## Against defaults

shadcn's button: `h-9 px-4 py-2 rounded-md text-sm font-medium`, solid near-black primary, `outline`/`ghost`/`destructive`/`link` variants, `sm`/`lg`/`icon` sizes, a ring on focus and `opacity-50` when disabled, a spinner when loading.

- Heather fill, not near-black or indigo: "one accent, heather … for primary actions"; banned "the 8px-grid indigo button".
- Two intents, no size prop: density sets size ([ADR 0001]); "fewer variants" is this skill's rule, the brief names only primary actions and the secondary control edge.
- 6px `rounded-control`, never a pill: radius table.
- Weight 600 from `text-label`, not 500: "weights 400 and 600 only".
- Disabled is a neutral colour role, not opacity: "`disabled` and its text are a flat, quiet neutral" (ADR 0002 bans `opacity-*`).
- Pending is a progress edge, not a spinner: "the one loop"; spinners loop by default with no fill.

- Horizontal padding 16px and centred label: matches the default; the brief is silent.

# Button: component plan

**Use**: the one action a person takes from here: approve, pay, save, send. Reach for `primary` for the single main action on a screen or bar, `secondary` for the rest. Not for navigation (a link) or for filters (segmented filter).

## Anatomy

A native `<button>`, no Radix primitive: a button has no behaviour Radix adds. `tv()` slots:

- `root`: the button.
- `icon`: optional leading Phosphor icon (regular weight), `aria-hidden`.
- `label`: the visible text; it is the accessible name.
- `edge` and `sweep`: the pending progress edge along the bottom (only while pending).

## Variants, sizes, states

- **`intent`: `primary` | `secondary`.** Brief: "one accent, heather … for primary actions"; `control` is "the 3:1 edge of an input or secondary button". No ghost, no destructive: the brief names neither (see GAPS).
- **No size prop.** Size follows the density set ([ADR 0001](../../../../docs/adr/0001-density-by-audience.md)): `text-label` 14/16px, `min-h-target` 24/44px, `size-icon` 16/20px.
- **States**, each visibly distinct from rest:
  - rest; hover (deeper fill); pressed (deeper still); focus-visible (2px heather outline, offset 2px);
  - disabled: flat quiet neutral fill and text, edge dropped ("`disabled` and its text are a flat, quiet neutral");
  - pending: keeps its intent colours, ignores hover/press, shows the progress edge ("a pending action shows a progress edge along its button's bottom").

## Token map

| Slot · state | primary | secondary |
|---|---|---|
| root, base | `relative inline-flex min-h-target min-w-target items-center justify-center gap-2xs overflow-hidden rounded-control border px-sm py-3xs text-label transition-colors duration-fast ease-standard focus-visible:focus-ring` | same |
| root, rest | `border-transparent bg-accent text-on-accent` | `border-control bg-surface text-ink` |
| root, hover | `hover:bg-accent-hover` | `hover:bg-surface-hover` |
| root, pressed | `active:bg-accent-pressed` | `active:bg-surface-pressed` |
| root, disabled | `border-transparent bg-disabled text-disabled cursor-not-allowed` | same |
| root, pending | `cursor-progress`, no hover/pressed classes | same |
| icon | `size-icon shrink-0` | same |
| edge | `absolute inset-x-0 bottom-0 h-edge origin-left animate-progress-fill overflow-hidden` | same |
| sweep | `block size-full bg-on-accent animate-progress-sweep` | `… bg-accent …` |

## A11y contract

- Role `button` (native); accessible name is the label text; the icon is `aria-hidden`.
- Enter and Space activate (native). Focus ring on `:focus-visible` only, never on click.
- Disabled: native `disabled`, out of the tab order; nothing to announce.
- Pending: `aria-busy="true"` and `aria-disabled="true"`, stays focusable so keyboard focus doesn't drop to the page mid-operation; clicks are swallowed.
- Target: `min-h-target min-w-target`, 24px admin (rendered 30px tall), 44px contractor.

## Motion

- Hover and press: background colour over `duration-fast` + `ease-standard` ("fast 120ms: press, hover colour").
- Pending: `edge` fills once over `slow` (`animate-progress-fill`), then `sweep` slides along it until `pending` turns false (`animate-progress-sweep`). The brief's one loop.
- Reduced motion: tokens.css strips animations, so the edge renders full and still ("a static edge"); colour changes stay a `fast` crossfade.

## Against defaults

shadcn's button: `h-9 px-4 py-2 rounded-md text-sm font-medium`, solid near-black primary, `outline`/`ghost`/`destructive`/`link` variants, `sm`/`lg`/`icon` sizes, a ring on focus and `opacity-50` when disabled, a spinner when loading.

- Heather fill, not near-black or indigo: "one accent, heather … for primary actions"; banned "the 8px-grid indigo button".
- Two intents, no size prop: density sets size ([ADR 0001]); "fewer variants" is this skill's rule, the brief names only primary actions and the secondary control edge.
- 6px `rounded-control`, never a pill: radius table.
- Weight 600 from `text-label`, not 500: "weights 400 and 600 only".
- Disabled is a neutral colour role, not opacity: "`disabled` and its text are a flat, quiet neutral" (ADR 0002 bans `opacity-*`).
- Pending is a progress edge, not a spinner: "the one loop"; spinners loop by default with no fill.
- Focus outline on `:focus-visible` only: matches shadcn's modern default; the brief demands it too.
- Horizontal padding 16px and centred label: matches the default; the brief is silent.

# Button: gaps

Places the brief, ADRs or tokens didn't decide something Button needed, the call made, and the alternative.

1. **Button height has no token.** The brief sets a minimum target (24/44px) but no button height. Call: `min-h-target` + `py-3xs` + `text-label` line height, which renders 30px on admin and 44px on contractor. Alternative: a `--height-control` density token (e.g. 32/44px) shared with inputs and segmented filters, so controls in one row line up.
2. **Horizontal padding doesn't follow density.** No density token for control padding, so both densities use `px-sm` (16px). Alternative: a density padding token (12px admin, 16–20px contractor).
3. **No destructive or quiet (ghost) intent.** The brief names only primary actions and the secondary control edge, and status colours "never borrow the accent", which suggests they aren't action colours either. Call: two intents. Alternative: a `danger` intent on its own role pair (e.g. for "Void invoice"), and a quiet intent for toolbar actions. Both need new colour roles first.
4. **Pending label and announcement.** The brief defines the progress edge but not whether the label changes ("Paying…") or how screen readers hear progress. Call: the label stays as written, the button gets `aria-busy` + `aria-disabled` and stays focusable. The result is announced by whatever confirms it (the toast). Alternative: a polite live region inside Button, or a `pendingLabel` prop.
5. **Disabled semantics.** Unstated. Call: native `disabled` (out of the tab order); pending uses `aria-disabled` so focus doesn't drop mid-operation. Alternative: `aria-disabled` for disabled too, so a keyboard user can reach the button and hear why it's unavailable. That needs a description pattern the library doesn't have yet.
6. **Sweep restart.** The tokens give two keyframes: fill (scaleX 0→1) and sweep (translateX −100%→100%, starting at 320ms). Nested, the edge fills, then visibly jumps from full to empty as the sweep begins. Alternative: a sweep keyframe starting at `translateX(0)`, or a narrower sweep segment, which is a tokens change.
7. **Edge sits inside the border.** `overflow-hidden` clips to the padding box, so on `secondary` the 2px heather edge sits on top of the 1px `control` border. Accepted at this size. Alternative: drop the bottom border while pending, which needs a `border-b-transparent`-style call the brief doesn't make.
8. **Icons.** There's no Icon component or icon registry, and a ReactNode can't be expressed in the Zod registry. Call: an `icon` prop that's an enum over a small Phosphor map (`check`, `download`, `send`, `plus`), leading only. Alternative: an `icon` slot taking a future Icon node, with the name list owned by Icon's registry entry.
9. **Registry `slots`.** ADR 0004 names slots for child nodes; Button has none (text is a `label` prop, per "every user-facing string is a literal prop"). Call: `slots: []`. The `tv()` slots (`root`, `icon`, `label`, `edge`, `sweep`) are internal parts, not registry slots.
10. **No full-width option.** Contractor screens on a phone often want a full-width primary. Call: none, until a layout component (Stack) can stretch its children. Alternative: a `width: "fit" | "fill"` prop.

- **Six stories**, with copy like "Approve and pay", "Request changes", "Pay 3 invoices" and "Send reminder".
- The registry reads its `intent` and `icon` options from the component's own config, so the two can't drift. It's exported from `src/index.ts`.

**Screenshot review:** I opened all 96 shots. The only change it led to was the "remove one accessory" step: I dropped the pointer cursor at rest, since the hover colour already shows it's clickable. A second pass found nothing more to change. The faint outline in the hover and pressed shots comes from the test harness, which tabs to the button before hovering; the component doesn't draw it.

- **No height or padding tokens for controls.** I used the minimum target size plus padding (30px admin), and 16px side padding at both densities.
- **Only two intents.** There's no destructive or quiet variant, because the brief names no colours for them.
- **The pending edge has two visual flaws.** The edge visibly jumps from full to empty when the sweep starts. On `secondary` it also sits on top of the grey bottom border. Fixing the jump needs a change to the keyframes in the tokens.
- **Pending and disabled behave differently.** Pending keeps the label as written and stays focusable. Disabled uses the native attribute, so it drops out of the tab order.
- **Icons are a small fixed list.** `check`, `download`, `send` and `plus`, because there's no Icon component to take them yet.

**Gaps** (10, in `GAPS.md`), the ones most worth your call first:
- **No height or padding tokens for controls.** I used the minimum target size plus padding (30px admin), and 16px side padding at both densities.
